correctness.rationale: For all n>=3, every normalized symmetric increasing function has nonnegative Hamming-threshold increments of total mass <=1. The conditioned four-term Walsh computation gives c_t=-F_(n-1)(t-1)/(2^n(n-1)(n-2)). An exact adjacent-difference factorization shows the only positive peaks and central negative valleys; the full feasible coefficient interval yields the sharp opposing-endpoint product and the convex-hull equality class. Local binomial asymptotics establish -exp(-3/2)/(6pi). check_level3.py independently checks all threshold identities through n=120 (7,257 cases), exact pairwise optima and small-cube Walsh sums; these checks supplement the all-n proof.

originality.rationale: A direct comparison of mathematical implications found no exact bounded symmetric sharp negative third-level cross-correlation constant or full extremizer classification in inspected sources. Recent Chang–Li–Wang–Wang derives a nonsharp-to-this-problem general W1/variance-dependent inequality and asks an independent ratio optimization question. The older Bernasconi paper already contains the single-threshold Krawtchouk formula, which is acknowledged rather than claimed; discrete opposing peaks, joint optimization, all equality cases and dimension-free limit are added here. Relevant unindexed or uninspected equivalents remain a stated bibliographic risk.
residual_risks: The indexed search and available full text do not exclude an older, unindexed equivalent optimization of symmetric threshold Krawtchouk coefficients.
The full text of arxiv:2606.08958 and arxiv:2610.16069 was not inspected; their available abstracts are not evidence of whole-document noncoverage.
No independent audit has been performed.

value.rationale: The third-level signed Fourier correlation of increasing functions is a central object in recent correlation inequalities. The sharp complete finite-dimensional negative frontier for bounded symmetric inputs, all extremal monotone threshold mixtures, and a nonzero dimension-free Gaussian limit isolate which threshold scales create maximal spectral anticorrelation. This is a natural complete classification across all dimensions rather than a small arbitrary example; it also distinguishes absolute spectral anticorrelation from the known first-level/variance-dependent inequality.
